04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma received a message from Fiona Bell the next morning. The records team had found a small book labelled “Outgoing letters — Student Travel 2011”. Fiona said it looked like a register used by the scheme administrator.

“Does it tell us which students received a letter?” Emma asked.

“Not exactly. Some lines contain dates and reference numbers. Others are blank. We have not compared the book with the original letters.”

“Can you tell me how many entries there are?”

“Not yet. The team needs to check the pages carefully. And we cannot share students’ personal details.”

Emma thanked her. She wrote register found in her notebook, but refused to write letters delivered. A list of letters prepared for sending was not proof that they reached anyone.

She called Sarah. Sarah wanted to know whether the book solved the mystery of the parent’s complaint.

“No,” Emma said. “We still do not know whether that parent received a decision. We don't even know whether the parent had applied.”

Fiona sent a photograph of the register’s cover and a blank page that showed its headings. There were four columns: reference number, date prepared, date sent and notes. The photograph did not show any student entries.

Emma noticed something useful. The two date columns were different. It seemed possible for a letter to be prepared on one day and sent on another. It was also possible for the second date to remain empty.

Later, the newspaper archive replied to Emma’s earlier enquiry. Staff had not yet checked the private letters from 2011. They reminded her that access might be restricted. Emma decided not to rely on material she had not seen.

In the afternoon Fiona called again. The team had begun making an inventory of the register. They could confirm that some rows contained dates in the sent column, but they could not say whether the letters had arrived. No postal receipts had been identified.

Sarah sighed when Emma told her. “So we finally have proof the letters were delivered?”

“Not delivered. At most, the register says that some were marked as sent.”

Emma thought about Claire. The teacher had worried about promises made to students. Now Emma was investigating the difference between written procedures and what happened in practice. The distinction mattered even if the records eventually showed no misconduct.

Before closing her notebook, Emma drew three short lines:

Prepared. Sent. Received.

She had evidence that the trust used those first two labels. For the third, she had nothing yet.

At the bottom of the page she added a new question: Who was responsible for checking whether a student received a decision?
